newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech leaders to change cabinet, no deal on seats.
newsitem.headline: Czech leaders to change cabinet, no deal on seats.

text.p: Leaders of the three parties in the ruling Czech coalition agreed on Wednesday to make changes in the makeup of the cabinet, but there was no deal yet on which positions would be affected, Czech Radio reported.

A brief joint statement of leaders of the three parties in the centre-right coalition said only that a late night meeting had ended in an agreement that a change in the composition of the cabinet was necessary.

The hastily-arranged meeting headed by Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, leader the senior Civic Democratic Party (ODS), came as criticism of post-Communist Europe's most durable governing coalition gathered pace.

Approval ratings for the government and especially Klaus's ODS have dropped recently because of a slowdown in economic performance, some highly publicised cases of financial crime and problems in the health care and education sectors.

Macroeconomic problems -- mainly a current account deficit of more than nine percent of gross domestic product and falling industrial output -- have cut the value of the Czech crown on foreign exchange markets.
The currency has also been hit by worries about political instability. The central bank intervened several times last week to support it.

Czech Radio quoted sources close to the talks as saying that one proposal under discussion was for Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec to replace Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik, with the former ambassador to the United States, Michael Zantovsky, then taking over as foreign minister.
This report could not be independently confirmed.

Zantovsky, the newly-installed chairman of the junior Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) who does not hold a ministerial seat, joined the late night meeting along with Agriculture Minister Josef Lux who heads the Christian Democratic Union and key deputies of each party.
Zantovsky was a former spokesman for President Vaclav Havel in the aftermath of the 1989 democratic revolution, and previously was a Prague-based correspondent for Reuters.
A regular meeting of the cabinet is scheduled for later on Wednesday.
Thirty five percent of respondents in a poll released on Monday said they trusted the government, down from 38 percent in April and 47 percent a year ago.
Kocarnik, who is also one of three deputy prime ministers along with Lux and Zieleniec, was chiefly blamed for the country's problems in the poll on Monday, with 28 percent saying he should resign.
Second in the unpopularity stakes was Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy of the ODA, with 22 percent saying he should quit.
Eighteen percent said Klaus should go.

Last month, Klaus announced a package of measures aimed at giving fresh impetus to economic growth, curbing trade and current account deficits and clamping down on economic crime. It included cuts in public spending and limits on wage growth.
